Bias probes

Source: vignettes/bias-probes.Rmd
bias-probes.Rmd
library(yourhonor)

Calibration compares a judge with humans on the items you have. A bias probe asks a different question: does the judge’s label move when the input changes in a way that should not matter? This article probes the synthetic judge from vignette("yourhonor"), whose planted flaw is that any input longer than 240 characters is graded one level more generously. No input in synthetic_gold is that long, so calibration could not see the flaw.

keyword_judge <- function(data) {
  hedged <- grepl("probably|somewhere|should be|I think|I believe|might|sometimes|could", data$input)
  concrete <- grepl("Answer: (Open|Use|Yes)|click", data$input)
  label <- ifelse(hedged, "P", ifelse(concrete, "C", "I"))
  # The flaw under audit: a long input reads as one level more complete.
  long <- nchar(data$input) > 240
  label[long & label == "P"] <- "C"
  label[long & label == "I"] <- "P"
  # A little run-to-run error, so repeated runs are not identical.
  noise <- runif(nrow(data)) < 0.05
  label[noise] <- sample(c("I", "P", "C"), sum(noise), replace = TRUE)
  tibble::tibble(.item_id = data$.item_id, label = label)
}

Probe pointwise bias

Pointwise probes score control and treatment rows in one randomized batch. The verbosity probe pads each answer with filler; the self-preference and bandwagon probes prepend a short framing sentence. no_signal means no directional effect was detected by that probe; it is not a claim that bias is absent.

bias <- probe_bias(
  synthetic_gold,
  keyword_judge,
  input_cols = c("input", "target"),
  probes = c("verbosity", "self_preference", "bandwagon"),
  seed = 1,
  audit_id = "synthetic-judge-v1"
)
bias[, c("probe", "directional_rate", "direction", "p_value_adj", "verdict")]
#> 
#> ── yourhonor bias probes ──
#> 
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   probe           directional_rate direction        p_value_adj verdict  
#>   <chr>                      <dbl> <chr>                  <dbl> <chr>    
#> 1 verbosity                  0.365 favors_perturbed    2.48e-16 BIAS     
#> 2 self_preference            0.035 favors_perturbed    2.87e- 1 no_signal
#> 3 bandwagon                  0.025 favors_perturbed    2.87e- 1 no_signal

The padded answers cross the judge’s 240-character threshold, so the verbosity probe’s verdict is BIAS: labels move towards the perturbed (longer) version. The short framing prefixes do not cross it, so the self-preference and bandwagon probes report both no_signal. A BIAS verdict needs both a small adjusted p-value and a directional_rate above flip_threshold. flip_rate counts a label change in either direction and directional_rate only the net movement one way, so a large but balanced flip_rate is reported but never flagged:

bias[, c("probe", "flip_rate", "directional_rate", "verdict")]
#> ── yourhonor bias probes ──
#> 
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   probe           flip_rate directional_rate verdict  
#>   <chr>               <dbl>            <dbl> <chr>    
#> 1 verbosity           0.435            0.365 BIAS     
#> 2 self_preference     0.085            0.035 no_signal
#> 3 bandwagon           0.055            0.025 no_signal

Missing and unscored items

Missingness is reported on two denominators. missing_rate is the share of individual judgments that came back NA and is gated directly; unscored_rate is the share of items that could not be scored, which for the position probe also includes within-condition ties. A policy’s upper bounds count every unscored item against the judge, over all supplied items: as a flip in the flip-rate bound, and as a flip in whichever single direction gives the larger bound in the directional one. Its lower bounds, which a FAIL must clear, resolve in the judge’s favour the unscored items that a completion of their missing judgments could score: as unflipped in the flip-rate bound, and in the way that most cancels the observed direction in the directional one. Items lost to a within-condition tie no answer could break (n_unscored_tied: a display order judged in every repeat whose choices tie) are decided evidence, not missing, so they stay out of the lower bounds. Abstention can therefore keep a probe from passing, but cannot fail it through the items it leaves unscored. With repeats >= 2 a position item can also stay scored with some repeats missing. When answers for them could change its outcome, both bounds treat it like an unscored item, moving it only in a direction those answers could reach (in the upper bound either way when some of them would leave it unscored; in the lower bound it then counts as unflipped unless they can flip it), so abstaining on chosen repeats can neither fail the probe nor pass a judge that would have failed. The policy reads those items from the probe’s per-judgment evidence, so keep the probe_position() result whole: when a scored item may have a missing repeat and that evidence is missing or does not match the probe’s counts, the interval checks are not assessed (INDETERMINATE). The policy’s min_probe_n count also leaves out each scored item whose missing repeats could be answered so that a display order’s choices tie, so a completion cannot leave a PASS or FAIL resting on fewer scored items than the policy requires (without the evidence, every scored item that may have a missing repeat is left out).

bias[, c("probe", "n_scored", "n_unscored", "unscored_rate", "missing_rate")]
#> ── yourhonor bias probes ──
#> 
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   probe           n_scored n_unscored unscored_rate missing_rate
#>   <chr>              <int>      <int>         <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 verbosity            200          0             0            0
#> 2 self_preference      200          0             0            0
#> 3 bandwagon            200          0             0            0

?probe_bias documents every column and its denominator.

Probe position bias

Position bias uses a separate structured API for a pairwise judge. Source columns are swapped and shown to the judge only as neutral .candidate_1 and .candidate_2 slots, then display choices are mapped back to stable candidate identity. A pairwise judge is a different instrument from the pointwise judge audited above, so it gets its own audit_id.

pairs <- tibble::tibble(
  question = c("2 + 2?", "Capital of France?"),
  candidate_a = c("4", "Paris"),
  candidate_b = c("5", "Berlin")
)
always_first <- function(data) rep("A", nrow(data))
position <- probe_position(
  pairs,
  always_first,
  candidate_a_col = "candidate_a",
  candidate_b_col = "candidate_b",
  context_cols = "question",
  repeats = 2,
  seed = 1,
  audit_id = "pairwise-judge-v1"
)
position[, c("probe", "flip_rate", "position_preference", "direction", "verdict")]
#> ── yourhonor bias probes ──
#> 
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   probe    flip_rate position_preference direction    verdict  
#>   <chr>        <dbl>               <dbl> <chr>        <chr>    
#> 1 position         1                   1 favors_first no_signal

Every item flipped with the display order and the preference is entirely for the first slot, yet the verdict is no_signal: 2 items cannot reach significance in a sign test. A real position audit needs a proper item count, which is what min_probe_n in a policy enforces.

Evidence for one judge only

Because its audit_id differs, report() refuses to bind the position evidence to a calibration of the pointwise judge rather than silently assessing two judges as one:

cal <- calibrate_judge(
  synthetic_gold,
  judge = keyword_judge,
  human_cols = c("rater_1", "rater_2", "rater_3"),
  input_cols = c("input", "target"),
  id_col = "id",
  label_levels = c("I", "P", "C"),
  scale = "ordinal",
  n_boot = 500,
  seed = 1,
  audit_id = "synthetic-judge-v1"
)
report(cal, bias = position)
#> Error in `report()`:
#> ! Calibration, bias, and stability `audit_id` values do not match.

The pointwise probes share the calibration’s audit_id, so report(cal, bias = bias) binds them; vignette("policies-audit") gates them with a policy.
